Cell-type-specific mixture exposure analysis

Source: R/mixture.R
run_sc_mixture.Rd

Estimates the relative contribution of multiple correlated exposures to gene expression within a specific cell type using a simplified quantile-scored linear model on pseudobulk data.

Usage

run_sc_mixture(
  x,
  exposures,
  celltype,
  celltype_col = "cell_type",
  target_genes = NULL,
  covariates = NULL,
  q = 4L,
  min_cells = 10L
)

Arguments

x

A SingleCellExposomeExperiment. Each cell's donor is read from the colData column named by sampleColumn(x).

exposures

Character vector. Exposure variable names, distinct. Each name must be a syntactic R name (see make.names) because it goes into the model formula, and cannot be y, the name of the response. Nor can it be ., ... or a name such as ..1, which R reads specially in a formula.

celltype

Character. Which cell type to analyse.

celltype_col

Character. colData column with cell type labels. Default "cell_type".

target_genes

Character vector (optional). Genes to test. Default: top 20 most variable genes.

covariates

Character vector (optional). Additional covariates from exposureData; a name that is not a column of exposureData is an error, and so is an exposure listed here. Names must be syntactic and cannot be y, ., ... or a name such as ..1, as for exposures.

q

Integer. Number of quantile bins, at least 2. Default 4. Tied exposure values (for example at a limit of detection) can give fewer bins.

min_cells

Integer. Minimum cells per donor. Default 10.

Value

A DataFrame with one row per target gene with a fitted model: gene and mixture_effect (the sum of that gene's estimable quantile-scored exposure coefficients; NA when none is estimable). metadata(result) holds:

weights

Named numeric vector. Relative contribution of each exposure (the weights that are not NA sum to 1): the mean over target genes of the absolute coefficients of the quantile-scored exposures, normalised. When the quantile scores of exposures are collinear, for example for two exposures with the same ranks, lm() estimates a coefficient only for the one listed first in exposures; it carries their joint effect, and the later ones get the weight NA, with a warning. When no coefficient can be estimated, every weight is NA.

mixture_coef

Overall mixture coefficient (sum of quantile-scored exposure coefficients, averaged across target genes); NA when no coefficient can be estimated.

method

Character. Always "quantile_linear".

celltype

Character. Cell type analysed.

n_donors

Integer. Donors with complete exposure and covariate data used in the analysis.

n_genes

Integer. Genes with a fitted model.

Details

This is a simplified screening method, not a formal quantile-based g-computation (Keil et al. 2020) or weighted quantile sum regression (Carrico et al. 2015). The approach:

  1. Donors with a missing exposure or covariate are removed, and exposures are scored into quantile bins (1 to q; fewer when quantiles are tied).

  2. For each target gene, a linear model is fit on pseudobulk log-CPM with all quantile-scored exposures and covariates as predictors.

  3. Weights are the absolute coefficients of the exposures that have one, averaged across target genes and normalised to sum to 1; an exposure without an estimable coefficient gets the weight NA (see Value). Because every exposure is on the same quantile scale, the coefficients are directly comparable.

Limitations:

  • No bootstrap confidence intervals on weights.

  • Does not separate positive/negative weight directions as in formal qgcomp.

  • Log-CPM may have heteroscedasticity at low counts.

For rigorous mixture analyses suitable for publication, consider qgcomp::qgcomp.noboot() or gWQS::gwqs() applied to the pseudobulk counts returned by donor_pseudobulk, or run_mixture_qgcomp.

References

Keil AP et al. (2020). A quantile-based g-computation approach to addressing the effects of exposure mixtures. Environ Health Perspect 128:047004. doi:10.1289/EHP5838

Carrico C et al. (2015). Characterization of weighted quantile sum regression for highly correlated data in a risk analysis setting. J Agric Biol Environ Stat 20:100-120.

Examples

library(SingleCellExperiment); library(S4Vectors)
set.seed(1)
counts <- matrix(rpois(5000, 8), nrow = 50,
    dimnames = list(paste0("G", 1:50), paste0("c", 1:100)))
sce <- SingleCellExperiment(assays = list(counts = counts),
    colData = DataFrame(cell_id = paste0("c", 1:100),
        donor_id = rep(paste0("D", 1:10), each = 10),
        cell_type = rep(c("Mono", "NK"), 50)))
exp_mat <- matrix(rnorm(30), nrow = 10,
    dimnames = list(paste0("D", 1:10), c("E1", "E2", "E3")))
scee <- build_scee(sce, exp_mat, sample_col = "donor_id")
mix <- run_sc_mixture(scee, exposures = c("E1", "E2", "E3"),
    celltype = "Mono", celltype_col = "cell_type",
    min_cells = 3L)
metadata(mix)$weights
#>        E1        E2        E3 
#> 0.3857350 0.2803696 0.3338954
